title: The Class That Was Rewritten: One Run Through attrs
premise:
Writing a Python class with a handful of data fields means hand-writing nine or more dunder methods 



 `__init__`, `__repr__`, `__eq__`, `__ne__`, ordering, hashing, pickling 



 and keeping them in sync forever. *attrs* offers to write them for you. The price is that a decorator gets to inspect your class body at import time and, for slotted classes, hand you back a *different class object* than the one you wrote. This story follows one real run of the README example: a class body with two annotated fields walks into `@define`, comes out as a finished, slotted, unhashable class; an instance of it is compared and serialized to a dict; and finally a second class is conjured at runtime from nothing but two strings. The reader is the person who has to sign off on all of that: what is guaranteed, what is silently decided, and where it can bite.

chapters.title: The Door, and the Flags That Become Policy
chapters.data_in: `class SomeClass` with annotations `a_number: int = 42` and `list_of_numbers: list[int] = Factory(list)`, handed to `@define` as `maybe_cls`
chapters.data_out: `ClassProps(is_exception=False, is_slotted=True, has_weakref_slot=True, is_frozen=False, kw_only=NO, collected_fields_by_mro=True, added_init=True, added_repr=True, added_eq=True, added_ordering=False, hashability=UNHASHABLE, added_match_args=True, added_str=False, added_pickling=True, on_setattr_hook=<wrapped_pipe>, field_transformer=None)`
inputs: Factory(list) as the default of list_of_numbers
facts: `Factory(list)` is evaluated at class-body time and merely stores the callable and `takes_self=False`; nothing is called yet (trace lines 2-3).

`define` defaults differ from `attr.s`: `slots=True`, `auto_exc=True`, `auto_detect=True`, `order=False`, `force_kw_only=False` 



 visible in the trace's argument list on line 4.

`wrap` mutates the decorator's own `on_setattr`: when the class is not frozen and the caller passed nothing, it installs `pipe(convert, validate)`, so by default assignment after construction re-runs converters and validators.

`wrap` walks `cls.__bases__` and, if any base has `__setattr__ is _frozen_setattrs`, inherits frozen-ness and forces `on_setattr = NO_OP`; if the caller had explicitly asked for an on_setattr hook, this combination raises `ValueError` instead of silently ignoring it.
`auto_attribs` was left `None`, so attrs guesses: it calls `do_it(cls, True)` first and only falls back to `do_it(cls, False)` if `UnannotatedAttributeError` is raised.

`auto_detect=True` means every `None` flag is resolved by asking `_has_own_attribute(cls, dunder)` 



 a check of `cls.__dict__` only, so an inherited `__eq__`/`__init__` does *not* stop attrs from writing its own (trace lines 15-26).

Hashability is derived, not asked for: `hash is None` + `eq True` + `frozen False` 



 `UNHASHABLE`. The class will be deliberately made un-hashable, matching Python's rule that customizing equality invalidates identity hashing.
`added_pickling` defaults to the value of `slots`, so slotted classes get `__getstate__`/`__setstate__` written unless `auto_detect` finds the user's own.

`cache_hash=True` with a non-hashable outcome is rejected with `TypeError` before any class is built 



 a road not taken here because `cache_hash=False`.
The resolved `ClassProps` is stored on the class as `__attrs_props__`, which is what `attrs.inspect()` later reads back.

open_questions.question: A convert-and-validate hook is now wired into every future attribute assignment. Does every instance pay for it, even though this class has no converters and no validators?
The auto_attribs guess is a try/except around the entire class build. What exactly triggers the fallback, and can a half-built class leak out of the failed attempt?
`hashability=UNHASHABLE` is a decision made for the user. What is physically done to the class, and can a base class's `__hash__` survive it?
`added_pickling=True` was chosen because the class is slotted. What exactly gets written, and what does it do with state it doesn't recognize?

chapters.title: Harvesting the Fields
chapters.data_in: `_transform_attrs(cls, these=None, auto_attribs=True, kw_only=KeywordOnly.NO, collect_by_mro=True, field_transformer=None)` over a class whose `__dict__` holds `42`, a `Factory`, and a method
chapters.data_out: `_Attributes(attrs=(Attribute(name='a_number', default=42, type=int, alias='a_number'), Attribute(name='list_of_numbers', default=Factory(list), type=list[int], alias='list_of_numbers')), base_attrs=[], base_attrs_map={})` wrapped in a generated `SomeClassAttributes` tuple subclass
facts: In `auto_attribs` mode the *annotations* drive the field list; a bare class attribute without an annotation is invisible, and plain values (`42`) are auto-wrapped by `attrib()` into a `_CountingAttr` (trace lines 37-50).

`_is_class_var` decides ClassVar-ness by **string matching** the annotation against `('typing.ClassVar', 't.ClassVar', 'ClassVar', 'typing_extensions.ClassVar')` 



 deliberately avoiding evaluation of string annotations, at the cost of being fooled by unusual aliasing.

The `UnannotatedAttributeError` that chapter 1's guess relies on is raised right here: any `attr.ib()`/`field()` in the class body without an annotation is collected into `unannotated` and rejected. The exception escapes before any class is created, so the retry in `wrap` starts from the untouched original class.

Because `collect_by_mro=True` (set unconditionally by `define`), base-class fields are gathered by reversed MRO and deduplicated, keeping only the freshest definition. `define` users never get the legacy ordering bug of issue #428.

Any field without an explicit alias gets `alias = name.lstrip('_')` and `alias_is_default = True`, written in via `object.__setattr__` because `Attribute` is frozen. This happens *before* `field_transformer` runs so hooks see usable aliases.

After the (absent) `field_transformer`, attrs enforces that no mandatory non-kw-only field follows one with a default 



 a `ValueError` at import time, not a `TypeError` at call time.

open_questions.question: Every field now carries an `alias` equal to its name minus leading underscores. Where does that string actually surface where a caller can see it?

answers.answer: `UnannotatedAttributeError` is raised inside `_transform_attrs`, before the builder touches the class; the `define.wrap` retry therefore re-enters with `auto_attribs=False` against a pristine class.

chapters.title: The Hook That Quietly Removed Itself
chapters.data_out: a builder whose `_on_setattr` is now `None`, holding `__attrs_attrs__`, `__attrs_props__`, getstate/setstate, a queued `__repr__` and `__eq__` script, `__ne__`, and `__hash__ = None`
facts:
The builder scans every field for a validator or converter; because `SomeClass` has neither, the class-level `pipe(convert, validate)` hook is dropped (`self._on_setattr = None`). The optimization applies only to the three known hooks `_DEFAULT_ON_SETATTR`, `setters.validate`, `setters.convert` 



 a custom callable is always kept.
`__attrs_attrs__` and `__attrs_props__` are placed on the class, which is the entire public introspection surface other tools (and `fields()`, `has()`, `inspect()`) rely on.

`slots_setstate` accepts both the modern dict state and a legacy tuple (pre-22.2.0 pickles), and silently skips names missing from the state 



 a slotted instance unpickled from an older/partial payload can come back with unset slots rather than an error.
For frozen classes the builder would instead install `_frozen_setattrs`/`_frozen_delattrs` here and mark `_wrote_own_setattr`; that branch was not taken.

The generated `__repr__` guards against infinite recursion using a thread-local set of `id(self)` (`_compat.repr_context.already_repring`); a self-referential object renders as `...` rather than blowing the stack. The thread-local lives in `_compat` so generated functions don't hold a direct reference to it, which would break cloudpickle.

`__eq__` begins with `if other.__class__ is not self.__class__: return NotImplemented` 



 equality is type-exact, so a subclass instance never compares equal to its base, by design. `__ne__` is a shared function that forwards `NotImplemented` rather than inverting it.

`add_setattr` finds no per-field `on_setattr` and a class hook of `None`, so `sa_attrs` is empty and it returns immediately: **this class gets no custom `__setattr__` at all** 



 assignments are ordinary slot writes.

`make_unhashable` sets `cls_dict['__hash__'] = None`, so `hash(instance)` raises `TypeError`. attrs only *adds*; if a base class defined a real `__hash__`, this `None` shadows it for this class but attrs never reaches up the MRO to remove anything.

open_questions.question:
Nothing executable has been produced yet 



 `__repr__` and `__eq__` are still strings. When and how do they become functions, and against which namespace?
`__eq__` short-circuits on exact class identity. What does that mean in practice for the comparisons the scenario actually performs?

answers.answer: No. Because no field has a converter or a validator, `_ClassBuilder.__init__` sets `self._on_setattr = None`, so the convert+validate hook is discarded before any `__setattr__` is written.
`make_unhashable` writes `__hash__ = None` into the class dict, so instances raise `TypeError` when hashed; it shadows rather than deletes any inherited `__hash__`.
`_make_getstate_setstate` returns `slots_getstate`/`slots_setstate` over the non-`__weakref__` field names; `slots_setstate` tolerates tuple state and missing keys.

chapters.title: Writing the Initializer, and Two Protocols Added Only If Vacant
chapters.data_in: `_make_init_script(cls, attrs, pre_init=False, post_init=False, frozen=False, slots=True, cache_hash=False, base_attr_map={}, is_exc=False, cls_on_setattr=None, attrs_init=False)`
chapters.data_out: init script `def __init__(self, a_number=attr_dict['a_number'].default, list_of_numbers=NOTHING): ... self.list_of_numbers = __attr_factory_list_of_numbers()` with globs including the defining module's `__dict__`; plus `cls_dict['__replace__']` and `cls_dict['__match_args__'] = ('a_number', 'list_of_numbers')`
inputs: the two Attributes with their defaults and aliases
facts:
The parameter names in the signature come from `a.alias`, not `a.name` 



 this is where chapter 2's underscore stripping becomes the public `__init__` contract.

A plain default is referenced indirectly as `attr_dict['a_number'].default`, so the `Attribute` object stays the single source of truth; a `Factory` default instead becomes `arg=NOTHING` plus an `if arg is not NOTHING: ... else: self.x = __attr_factory_x()`, which is why each instance gets a *fresh* list rather than a shared one.

Because the class is neither frozen nor hash-caching, `_determine_setters` returns the plain `_assign` strategy: the generated body is literally `self.a_number = a_number`. Frozen classes would instead go through a cached `object.__setattr__` or direct `__dict__` writes.

`_make_init_script` updates the generated function's globals with `sys.modules[cls.__module__].__dict__` so `typing.get_type_hints(C.__init__)` can resolve string annotations 



 a deliberate trade of namespace purity for working type resolution.

Validators, when present, are emitted as a single `if _config._run_validators is True:` block after all assignments, so validators see a fully populated instance and can be globally disabled at runtime.
`init=False` on the decorator would route the identical script to `__attrs_init__` instead, leaving the user's own `__init__` in place.

`__replace__` (the `copy.replace` protocol, 3.13+) is a thin proxy to `attrs.evolve`, which rebuilds the instance **through `__init__`** using each field's alias 



 so `init=False` fields cannot be replaced and all validators/converters re-run on the copy.
Both `__replace__` and `__match_args__` are skipped when the class defines its own in its own `__dict__`; inherited versions do not count. `__match_args__` lists only `init=True`, non-kw-only fields.
`_add_method_dunders_unsafe` rewrites `__module__`, `__qualname__` and `__doc__` on every attached method; the `_safe` variant suppresses `AttributeError` instead.

open_questions.question: The initializer's globals now include every name in the defining module. Is that live, and what is the blast radius if the module later rebinds a name?

answers.answer: The alias is used verbatim as the `__init__` parameter name in `_attrs_to_init_script` (`arg_name = a.alias`), which is why `_x` becomes `x` in the public signature.

chapters.title: One compile(), One linecache Entry
chapters.data_in: three queued snippets (repr, eq, init) with merged globs, filename `<attrs generated methods __main__.SomeClass>`
chapters.data_out: `locs = {'__repr__': <function>, '__eq__': <function>, '__init__': <function>}`, each attached to `cls_dict` with attrs-branded `__qualname__`/`__doc__`, and `__init__.__annotations__` set
inputs: the snippet list accumulated in chapters 3-4
facts:
All snippets are concatenated and compiled **once** per class, and their globs dicts are merged into a single namespace 



 so a name used by one generated method is visible to all of them.

The source is registered in `linecache.cache` under a synthetic filename, which is what lets a debugger step through `__init__` and tracebacks show real source lines; collisions append a counter until a free filename is found.

`eval` is called on compiled bytecode built from strings attrs itself constructed from field *names*. Field names come from the class body or from `make_class` 



 attrs explicitly documents that validating identifiers is the caller's duty, so a hostile or malformed name is an injection surface the library does not police.

The globs dict passed to `eval` becomes the function's `__globals__` 



 it is a live dict, but it was built by *copying* the module's `__dict__` at class-creation time, so later rebindings in the module are **not** seen by the generated code.
Attaching happens via per-snippet hooks (`_attach_repr`, `_attach_eq`, `_attach_init`) that pull the function out of the eval'd namespace and stamp it with the owning class's dunders.

open_questions.question:
These functions were compiled while the original class object still existed, and some of them (plus user methods) may hold it in a closure cell. The class is about to be replaced 



 what happens to those references?

answers.answer: `_eval_snippets` joins all snippets, compiles them once under a unique synthetic filename registered with `linecache`, and `eval`s them into a merged globals dict; the resulting functions are then attached to `cls_dict`.

It is a copy taken at class-creation time, not a live view of the module: `globs.update(sys.modules[...].__dict__)` snapshots the namespace, so later rebindings in the module don't reach the generated `__init__`.

chapters.title: The Class You Get Back Is Not the Class You Wrote
chapters.data_in: `cls_dict` (methods, `__attrs_attrs__`, `__attrs_props__`, getstate/setstate) plus the original `SomeClass` type object
chapters.data_out:
a brand-new `<class '__main__.SomeClass'>` with `__slots__ = ('a_number', 'list_of_numbers', '__weakref__')`, returned up through `attrs` 



 `do_it` 



 `wrap` 



 `define`; then `sc != SomeClass(2, [3, 2, 1])` 



 `True`
facts: Slotted classes cannot be retrofitted, so attrs builds a *new* type with the same name and bases and drops the field names into `__slots__`. The original class survives only as `OriginalCls.__attrs_base_of_slotted__`, a weak reference to the replacement.

Because of the swap, methods that used bare `super()` or `__class__` carry a closure cell pointing at the *old* class; `_create_slots_class` walks `cls.__dict__.values()` (unwrapping class/staticmethods and properties) and rewrites any cell whose contents are the old class. This is the documented fix for issue #102 and the reason `functools.cached_property` and bare `super()` keep working.

Only non-inherited names are slotted, and slots already defined by a base are re-bound from `existing_slots` rather than redefined, so parent descriptors aren't shadowed incorrectly. A `__weakref__` slot is added unless the class or an ancestor already has one.

Consequences of the swap are real and documented: `object.__init_subclass__` fires for both the old and the new class, and the dead original lingers in `type.__subclasses__` until a GC pass (issue #407).

After construction, `build_class` calls `cls.__attrs_init_subclass__()` if one is *inherited* (not defined on this class) 



 attrs' replacement for the `__init_subclass__` hook it breaks. The non-slotted path would instead call `_patch_original_class` and run `abc.update_abstractmethods`.

The trace shows exactly one attrs-owned function in the whole instance lifetime: `__ne__`. Construction, repr and `__eq__` are generated code living on the class, not library calls 



 the near-zero runtime overhead claim is visible here as an absence.

`__ne__` calls `self.__eq__(other)`, gets a real `False` (both operands are `SomeClass`), and returns `True`. Had the operands differed in class, `__eq__` would return `NotImplemented` and `__ne__` would forward it. `hard_math` is untouched user code.

open_questions.question: These instances have no `__dict__` at all. How does a helper like `asdict` find out what they contain?
All of this machinery ran off a class body written by hand. Can the same pipeline be driven at runtime from nothing but a list of names?

answers.answer: `_create_slots_class` iterates the new class's members plus the collected cached-property/`__getattr__` functions and rewrites every closure cell whose contents are the old class to point at the replacement.

Both comparisons in the scenario are between two `SomeClass` instances, so the identity check passes and the field-by-field chain decides; a differently-typed operand would yield `NotImplemented` instead of `False`.

chapters.title: Flattening It Out
facts:
The `attrs`-namespace `asdict` is a thin wrapper that hard-codes `retain_collection_types=True` and `dict_factory=dict`; the `attr`-namespace version defaults to flattening tuples/sets into lists. The two namespaces therefore produce *different* output for the same input 



 a deliberate 'nicer defaults' choice that matters when porting code.

`fields(inst.__class__)` reads `__attrs_attrs__` off the class, which is how a slotted instance with no `__dict__` is still fully enumerable; `fields` raises `NotAnAttrsClassError` for a plain class and `TypeError` for a non-class non-instance.

`asdict` reads values with `getattr(inst, a.name)` 



 the **field name**, not the alias 



 so private fields come out with their leading underscores.

Recursion is driven by `type(v)`: exact membership in `_ATOMIC_TYPES` short-circuits, then `has(value_type)` for nested attrs classes, then tuple/list/set/frozenset, then dict; anything else is passed through unchanged. `has()` also handles specialized generics (`A[str]`) by caching `__attrs_attrs__` onto the alias.

With `retain_collection_types=True`, the collection is rebuilt via `cf(items)` and falls back to `cf(*items)` only for tuple subclasses (namedtuples); a collection type whose constructor takes neither shape raises `TypeError` straight through.

The output list is a *new* list of the same elements 



 a shallow copy, so mutating a nested non-atomic element still reaches back into the original instance.
`filter` runs before `value_serializer`; both were `None` here, so neither code path was exercised.

open_questions.question: `asdict` in the `attrs` namespace quietly differs from `attr.asdict`. Does `make_class` sit on the modern defaults too, or on the legacy ones?

answers.answer: Through `fields(cls)`, which reads the `__attrs_attrs__` tuple that `_ClassBuilder` stamped onto the class; the instance's lack of `__dict__` is irrelevant because the field names come from the class and the values via `getattr`.

chapters.title: A Class From Two Strings
chapters.data_out: a fresh `type_` named `C` plus `these={'a': _CountingAttr(counter=8), 'b': _CountingAttr(counter=9)}`, handed to `attrs(these=..., slots=False, auto_detect=False, eq=True, order=True, force_kw_only=True)` which returns the `wrap` closure
facts:
The class name is normalized with `unicodedata.normalize('NFKC', name)` to match how Python parses identifiers; beyond that, `make_class` explicitly does **not** validate that the name or the attribute names are valid identifiers 



 invalid ones will surface as a `SyntaxError` from the generated-code `compile()`, not as a clear error here.
A list input becomes `{name: attrib()}` in order; a dict input is used as-is; anything else raises `TypeError`.
`__attrs_pre_init__`, `__attrs_post_init__` and `__init__` are *popped* out of the attrs dict and moved into the real class body, so they are treated as methods rather than fields.
`__module__` is patched from `sys._getframe(1)` so pickling works, with `AttributeError`/`ValueError` suppressed on interpreters without frame access.

`make_class` is a wrapper around `attr.s`, **not** `attrs.define`: the trace shows `slots=False`, `auto_detect=False`, `auto_exc=False`, `on_setattr=None`, `collect_by_mro` defaulting to False, and `order` resolved to `True`. Converters and validators will therefore *not* run on attribute assignment for classes made this way.
Annotations are attached to the finished class only afterwards (`cls.__annotations__ = {...}`), because setting them earlier would make `_transform_attrs` treat them as auto_attribs fields.

open_questions.question: `slots=False` this time. If attrs doesn't build a replacement type, what does it do to the class object it was handed?

`collect_by_mro` is left at its `attr.s` default of False. Does that change anything for a class with no attrs bases 



 and what would it change if there were any?

answers.answer:
Yes 



 `make_class` builds a bare type with `types.new_class`, synthesizes one `attrib()` per name, and pushes it through the exact same `attrs()` pipeline via the `these` argument.

chapters.title: The Same Machine, Legacy Settings
chapters.data_out: a builder for `C` carrying repr/eq/init snippets, four ordering methods, `__hash__ = None`, `__replace__`, and `__match_args__ = ('a', 'b')`; the init script is `def __init__(self, a, b): self.a = a; self.b = b`
facts:
With `these` supplied, `_transform_attrs` ignores the class body entirely and `_delete_attribs` is set False 



 attrs will not strip anything off the class. Annotations come back empty (trace lines 179-180).

`collect_by_mro=False` routes base-class collection through `_collect_base_attrs_broken`, which walks the MRO *forward*, includes already-inherited attributes and mutates `taken_attr_names`. It reproduces the known-wrong ordering of issue #428 on purpose, for backwards compatibility. Here both base lists are empty, so the choice is invisible 



 but it is the behaviour any `make_class` user inherits.

`order=True` adds `__lt__`, `__le__`, `__gt__`, `__ge__`, which build tuples of the ordered fields and return `NotImplemented` unless `other.__class__ is self.__class__` 



 subclasses are not comparable.
`add_setattr` again finds nothing to do, because `attr.s` leaves `on_setattr` at `None` by default: a `make_class` class never converts or validates on assignment, unlike a `define` class.
Both fields are mandatory with no converters, so the generated `__init__` is literally the two-line body a human would write, and `annotations` is just `{'return': None}`.
Ordering methods are attached directly to `cls_dict` (not compiled from a script), while repr/eq/init go through the snippet pipeline.

answers.answer: Legacy ones: `make_class` calls `_attrs` (`attr.s`), so `C` is a dict class with ordering, no `auto_detect`, no `auto_exc`, and no on_setattr hooks.

Nothing here 



 `_collect_base_attrs_broken` returns `([], {})` for a class whose only base is `object`; with real attrs bases it would collect in forward-MRO order and include already-inherited attributes, reproducing issue #428.

chapters.title: Patching In Place, and the Coda
chapters.data_in: the builder for `C` with its compiled `__repr__`/`__eq__`/`__init__` and the ordering/match-args entries
chapters.data_out:
`<class '__main__.C'>` 



 the *same* object `types.new_class` produced, now carrying all attrs methods; `C('foo','bar')` reprs as `C(a='foo', b='bar')`; final `sc.__ne__(SomeClass(2, [3, 2, 1]))` 



 `True`
facts:
For a non-slotted class, `_patch_original_class` mutates the class you handed in: it `setattr`s every entry of `cls_dict` onto it and returns the same object. No identity swap, no closure rewriting, no `__init_subclass__` double-fire 



 the gotchas of chapter 6 simply don't apply.
Field definitions would normally be deleted from the class body here, but `_delete_attribs` is False because `these` was used, so nothing is removed (the documented 18.1.0 behaviour).

If the class inherited an attrs-written `__setattr__` but this class doesn't write its own, `_patch_original_class` resets `__attrs_own_setattr__` to False and restores `object.__setattr__` 



 unless the user has a custom one. This is the only place an inherited hook is taken away.
`build_class` wraps the result in `abc.update_abstractmethods` so a patched class with newly-implemented abstract methods stops being abstract.

The run ends where it began: a shared `__ne__` returning `True`. Across both classes, the only attrs code executing after class creation was `__ne__` and `asdict` 



 every other guarantee was baked into generated functions at import time.

answers.answer: It mutates it: `_patch_original_class` sets every generated method onto the original class object and returns it, so `C` keeps its identity and none of the slotted-class replacement caveats apply.
